description:
I'm a Computer Science Engineering student passionate about artificial intelligence, machine learning, and software development.

I'm participating independently in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, focusing on "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!"

My goal is to explore NASA's Earth observation datasets and develop an AI-powered solution for analyzing environmental trends, detecting meaningful changes, and presenting insights through interactive visualizations.
summary: Drift is a browser-based Earth trend atlas that answers the four questions at the heart of this challenge: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. Users pick a NASA variable (GISTEMP v4 surface temperature or GPCP v2.3 precipitation), a season and any window of years, and Drift recomputes a trend and significance test for every grid cell on Earth in a second or two. It uses Sen's slope, the Mann–Kendall test with Hamed–Rao persistence correction, and Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery control, so faded cells mark change that could be noise and bold cells mark robust trends. Users can click a place or drag a region to see its time series, trend with 95% band and change point, and download the data. A Point lab adds humidity and wind from NASA POWER (MERRA-2) at eight places. Six detective case files, a guided tour and a plain-language Field Guide help students and the public become Earth data detectives.
details: WHAT IT DOESDrift turns NASA climate records into an interactive trend atlas. Pick a variable, a season (annual, Dec–Feb, Mar–May, Jun–Aug, Sep–Nov) and any window of years. Drift recomputes a trend and a significance test for every grid cell on Earth, in the browser, within a second or two. The headline answer, the share of Earth's surface that changed and the strongest regions are all written from the current result; none of the text is pre-written.HOW IT WORKS- Trend: Sen's slope (median of all pairwise slopes), robust to outliers.- Significance: Mann–Kendall test with tie correction, with the variance corrected for serial correlation (Hamed & Rao, 1998).- Slope interval: 95% confidence interval from ranked pairwise slopes.- Field significance: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (q = 0.10) across all cells, so the map does not overstate how much has changed.- Change point: Pettitt test for a selected place or region.- Regional means use cos(latitude) area weights.The statistics are tested against pymannkendall and scipy.stats.theilslopes reference values, including autocorrelated and heavily tied series.FEATURES- A spinning globe painted with the live result that unfolds into an Equal Earth map as you scroll.- A map of Sen's slope per decade where cells without a robust trend fade, so the real signal stands out.- Click a cell, drag a box or pick a hotspot to see its time series with climate stripes, fitted trend and 95% band, the year of the largest shift and a statistics table. Any series downloads as CSV with source and method in the header.- Year-by-year animation, a draggable timeline to choose the period, and shareable URLs.- Point lab: temperature, rainfall, relative humidity and wind speed from NASA POWER (MERRA-2) at eight contrasting places, with trend tests, false discovery control across places, a ranking, a map and CSV export.- Six detective case files (Arctic warming, Siberian winters, the North Atlantic cold blob, India's monsoon, the Sahel's recovery, opposite Pacific rainfall trends) that open the live analysis on a real question.- A ten-step guided tour, a step-by-step method explainer, and a Field Guide with plain-language definitions and animated diagrams for every variable and statistical term.- A latitude profile and connected regions of robust change in both directions, showing that one variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another.DATA PIPELINEA Python script downloads the original NASA NetCDF files, averages months into years and seasons (weighted by days per month) and stores compact int16 grids. Nothing is interpolated or filled in; cells with data in under 70% of the selected years are left blank.TOOLSJavaScript, HTML/CSS, D3, TopoJSON, Canvas/WebGL and Web Workers; Python with netCDF4 and NumPy for data processing; GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for testing and hosting. No backend, accounts or API keys.IMPACTDrift helps high school and college students and the interested public find what is changing, where and how fast, and tell real trends from noise. Its limits are stated openly: a robust trend shows a change is unlikely to be noise, not what caused it.USE OF AIAI coding assistants helped write parts of the code, documentation, slides and demo video, as noted in the project's README and About page. All scientific values come from NASA data and are checked against independent reference libraries.
